name_ar: أبو الوليد محمد بن أحمد بن رشد القرطبي
name_en: Abu al-Walid Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Rushd al-Qurtubi
epithet: Ibn Rushd (known in Western scholasticism as Averroes)
summary: Ibn Rushd (520–595 AH), known in Latin Christendom as Averroes, was a Cordoban Maliki jurist, physician, and the most influential philosopher of medieval Islam. His extensive commentaries on Aristotle, transmitted through Arabic into Latin, shaped the development of Scholastic philosophy and natural science in Europe for three centuries. His standing in Islamic scholarship is more complex: he was a trained Maliki jurist whose fiqh work Bidayat al-Mujtahid is a masterpiece of comparative jurisprudence, but his Aristotelian philosophical positions on the eternity of the world and related questions placed him in tension with mainstream Sunni theology — a tension his own teacher al-Ghazali had attacked philosophically a generation earlier.
biography:
Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Rushd was born in 520 AH (1126 CE) in Cordoba, al-Andalus, into a prominent family of Maliki scholars. His grandfather, also named Muhammad ibn Rushd (Abu al-Walid al-Jadd), was the Chief Qadi (Qadi al-Qudat) of Cordoba and one of the most eminent Maliki jurists of his generation. His father Ahmad ibn Rushd was also a Maliki judge. Ibn Rushd grew up in this intensely learned environment, receiving a thorough formation in Maliki fiqh, hadith, Arabic language, and medicine.

His philosophical development was shaped by an encounter with the Almohad ruler Abu Ya'qub Yusuf I (r. 558–580 AH), who reportedly commissioned him — through the intermediary of the philosopher Ibn Tufayl — to write clear commentaries on the works of Aristotle to make them accessible to the Arabic-speaking scholarly world. Ibn Rushd accepted this commission and over the following decades produced a series of short paraphrases (jawami), middle commentaries (talkhis), and long commentaries (tafsir/sharh) on virtually all of Aristotle's surviving works. These commentaries ranged from close technical analyses to reformulations of Aristotelian positions within the Arabic intellectual context. It is through these works that Ibn Rushd entered European intellectual history: translated into Latin in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, his commentaries were so influential that Scholastic philosophers (including Thomas Aquinas) simply referred to him as 'the Commentator' — as Aristotle was 'the Philosopher.' (Renan, Averroes et l'Averroisme — though a hostile 19th-century source, documents the Latin transmission)

In Maliki fiqh, Ibn Rushd produced Bidayat al-Mujtahid wa Nihayat al-Muqtasid (Beginning for the Independent Legal Thinker, End for the Moderate) — a two-volume comparative jurisprudence work that presents the positions of the major legal schools on every significant legal question, explains the textual and methodological reasons for their differences, and guides the reader in independent legal reasoning. This work is exceptional in the Islamic legal tradition for its explicit focus on the underlying sources of juristic disagreement rather than merely presenting conclusions. It remains a standard reference in Islamic legal education. (Ibn Rushd, Bidayat al-Mujtahid, Vol. 1, Introduction)

His Kulliyyat fi al-Tibb (Latin: Colliget) was a medical encyclopedia that, alongside Avicenna's Canon of Medicine, formed the foundation of European medical education for centuries. He also wrote extensively on astronomy, physics, psychology (in the Aristotelian sense), and metaphysics.

The philosophical positions for which Ibn Rushd is most debated within Islamic thought include: his defense of the Aristotelian doctrine of the eternity of the world (qidam al-alam) — the same position al-Ghazali had declared inconsistent with Islamic belief in his Tahafut al-Falasifah; his position on divine knowledge of particulars; and his views on the nature of the intellect. Ibn Rushd responded to al-Ghazali's Tahafut al-Falasifah in his Tahafut al-Tahafut (Incoherence of the Incoherence), defending the philosophers against al-Ghazali's critique. These positions on eternity and divine knowledge are incompatible with mainstream Sunni theology as understood by Athari, Ash'ari, and Maturidi scholars alike; al-Ghazali had specifically identified them as contradictions of Islamic belief.

His involvement with the Almohad court brought him both patronage and persecution. In 591 AH, for reasons that remain somewhat unclear — likely a combination of political pressures, religious conservatism at court, and the exposure of his philosophical positions to a wider audience — he was publicly denounced in Cordoba, his philosophical works were banned and burned, and he was exiled to Lucena (a town with a large Jewish population near Cordoba). He was rehabilitated shortly before his death. He died in Marrakesh in 595 AH (1198 CE).

Ibn Rushd's legacy is genuinely bifurcated: in Islamic jurisprudence, Bidayat al-Mujtahid is an acknowledged masterpiece read by Maliki and non-Maliki scholars alike for its comparative rigor. In philosophy, his Aristotelian commentaries had their greatest influence outside the Islamic world. Within Islamic intellectual history, his philosophical positions are not merely points of intra-Sunni scholarly contention. It should be noted that three of Ibn Rushd's positions — the eternity of the world, divine ignorance of particulars, and the denial of bodily resurrection — were specifically identified by al-Ghazali as contradictions of Islamic belief (not mere juristic disagreement), and this assessment has been shared by subsequent Athari, Ash'ari, and Maturidi scholarship. These positions are outside the bounds of Sunni aqeedah, not within its spectrum of accepted scholarly ikhtilaf.
key_works: Bidayat al-Mujtahid wa Nihayat al-Muqtasid (2 volumes — comparative Maliki fiqh)
Tahafut al-Tahafut (Incoherence of the Incoherence — response to al-Ghazali)
Commentaries on Aristotle (short, middle, and long formats — Physics, Metaphysics, Ethics, Rhetoric, Poetics, De Anima, and others)
Fasl al-Maqal (On the Harmony of Religion and Philosophy)
al-Kashf an Manahij al-Adillah (Uncovering the Methods of Proof — theology and philosophy)
